The story is tightly unified, with every scene and detail working together to serve the central narrative and theme. The opening establishes Ruth's physical and emotional exhaustion as well as the effects of the anesthesia and morphine. The middle section, featuring the disorienting hospital ward and the vignettes of the other confused, exhausted mothers, serves a dual purpose: it mirrors Ruth's own medicated haze and makes it entirely plausible that a baby mix-up could happen without anyone immediately noticing. Specific details introduced early on—such as the first nurse's comment that the baby was "clean as a whistle" and the baby's tiny four-pound weight—directly set up the climax at home when Ruth discovers the mole, the heavier weight, and the Lindqvist hospital band. Finally, Ruth's shocking decision to keep the switched baby is made psychologically believable by weaving in the backstory of her stressful, uncertain pregnancy, tying the plot directly into the overarching theme of "the weight of certainty."
